deep_why: The core problem is allocating multiple expert modules to many recommendation tasks without wasting computation or forcing unrelated tasks to share knowledge. The underlying principle is that orthogonal expert directions guarantee they cannot interfere with each other—if task A's best solution lies along one direction and task B's along a perpendicular direction, they can be learned independently without one corrupting the other. This principle applies because real recommendation tasks, though correlated, target different outcomes (clicks, shares, follows, dwell time) whose optimal solutions genuinely point in different feature spaces. By ensuring each task gets specialized experts arranged orthogonally while a small shared backbone routes flexibly, the system can scale to many tasks without the computation quadrupling with each new task—the hierarchy keeps the growth linear. This solves the real bottleneck: industrial short-video platforms cannot afford to double their compute budget every time a new interaction signal matters.

The core problem is that single-policy CTR models get trapped in local minima where small improvements stop happening. The underlying principle is that internal competition—having two sub-learners alternate as reference and target—creates a continuous gradient landscape that prevents settling, because one learner's success destabilizes the other's, forcing both to keep improving. This principle applies because having two models on the same data but with swapped roles (one must beat the other each batch) means neither can achieve static equilibrium; they naturally escape stagnation the way two animals competing for resources must keep evolving or lose access. The asymmetric gradient flow ensures the target learner moves toward beating the reference, which then adapts, creating a cycle that prevents saturation. This solves the practical goal: getting CTR models past the performance plateau where incremental gains have become impossibly small.

The core problem is that weak user feedback signals in reinforcement learning produce unstable gradient updates that push the model toward gaming the reward signal rather than learning genuine user preferences. The underlying principle is that filtering high-confidence conversion signals amplifies the gradient from trustworthy examples while dampening noisy ones, which stabilizes learning in the same way tuning down a feedback amplifier stops it from squealing. This principle applies because real click data contains massive noise—accidental clicks, bots, misattribution—but conversion events (actual purchases) are far more reliable indicators of true preference. By resampling to emphasize conversion intents and using a drift-limiting barrier that pulls the model back toward its starting behavior when it strays too far, the system keeps learning from good signal while rejecting bad signal. This solves the real challenge: enabling end-to-end learning for generative recommendation without the model collapsing into reward hacking.

The core problem is extracting structured question-answer pairs from unstructured Chinese text. The underlying principle is that code-based models, trained on vast software documentation where questions and answers are inherently paired and formatted in regular ways, have learned implicit structural patterns that generalize to any language containing similar logical sequences. This principle applies because code mirrors natural language structure—both have questions (comments asking what a function does) followed by answers (the function itself)—and models trained on code learn to recognize paired reasoning patterns more robustly than language-specific models trained only on native text. Expanding vocabulary to include Chinese characters lets the code-trained model apply its learned structural reasoning to Chinese, reducing hallucination because it already knows what a well-formed answer looks like. This solves the practical goal: building QA extraction that works across languages without requiring language-specific training data.

The core problem is deciding which ad to show in which slot on a multi-slot page to satisfy multiple advertiser contracts fairly while maximizing revenue. The underlying principle is that bipartite matching guarantees a globally optimal allocation exists and can be found efficiently if you frame the problem as a graph where viewers connect to slots and slots connect to ads—this graph structure makes the problem solvable exactly rather than requiring greedy approximations. This principle applies because the constraints (each advertiser has a fixed contract to fulfill, each viewer sees one page, each slot shows one ad) form clear logical boundaries that bipartite graphs are designed to represent. The roulette mechanism (randomly choosing from valid ads per slot) prevents some ads from dominating all slots while fulfilling their contracts. Solving this optimally rather than greedily prevents the most popular ads from monopolizing inventory. This solves the real problem: platform monetization—maximizing revenue fairly across many advertisers instead of letting a few take all the premium slots.

The core problem is matching viewers to streamers while respecting each streamer's service capacity—too many viewers overwhelms them and degrades quality for everyone. The underlying principle is that optimal subgraph selection on a bipartite graph guarantees the maximum viewer-streamer match that respects capacity is found globally, not just greedily; this is achievable because once you model capacity as an edge weight constraint, the problem becomes a classical graph optimization that algorithms can solve exactly. This principle applies because streamers truly have hard capacity limits—bandwidth, moderation ability, chat responsiveness—that degrade quality when exceeded, and viewers truly have clear preferences they'd like satisfied; the bipartite structure captures both. By learning capacity estimates and then finding the globally optimal subgraph, the system avoids the trap of greedily pushing all viewers toward popular streamers (which saturates them) while starving unpopular ones. This solves the practical goal: delivering good user experience and fair opportunity for all streamers simultaneously.

The core problem is inferring evolving user intent from recent behavior without sending data to a cloud server, which adds latency and cost. The underlying principle is that deploying a smaller capable model locally executes instantly on device, eliminating the round-trip time; smaller models achieve this by learning to focus on user intent signals rather than memorizing irrelevant patterns, so they still capture rapid preference shifts. This principle applies because user intent in e-commerce changes quickly—a shopper browsing skis one moment and swimsuits the next—and cloud round-trip latency (hundreds of milliseconds) is too slow to detect that shift; local instant inference adapts immediately. Smaller models deployed on-device work because intent is a concentrated signal (what the person wants right now) that doesn't require enormous capacity. This solves the practical goal: real-time personalization on mobile where network latency would otherwise force stale recommendations.

The core problem is generating item recommendations end-to-end while balancing reasoning depth (why this item?) with serving speed (show it now). The underlying principle is that splitting the system into a fast lightweight generator and a slow reasoning pipeline lets each use its strengths—the fast path handles 99% of users instantly, the slow path reasons about complex cases offline to guide it, and combining their outputs via tree search and multi-scenario optimization finds recommendations that satisfy all scenarios simultaneously. This principle applies because real e-commerce traffic is not homogeneous: some queries are simple (buy bestseller), others are complex (find gift for specific person), and no single model strikes the right speed-depth tradeoff for all; separating them lets each model do its job perfectly. Using tree search to explore candidate combinations finds Pareto-optimal solutions that don't sacrifice one scenario for another. This solves the practical goal: shipping a generative recommender that is both smart enough to handle complexity and fast enough to serve millions of users.

The core problem is predicting next user behavior (what they'll click, order) from their complex evolving interests without losing information or producing homogeneous predictions. The underlying principle is that multi-granularity reasoning—first predicting coarse-grained attributes in parallel, then refining to fine-grained item predictions, then expanding to order-level predictions—preserves complete user information at each step because you reason within the item space (where the data actually lives) rather than transforming to an intermediate representation and back, which always leaks details. This principle applies because user behavior has natural nested structure: they care about brand or category first (coarse), then specific items (fine), then patterns of items they buy together (order-level); reasoning through these layers sequentially without information loss lets each stage refine the previous one. Keeping reasoning implicit (in item space) rather than explicit text avoids the problem where intermediate reasoning steps are lossy. This solves the practical goal: generating predictions diverse enough to match real behavior—not homogeneous—while capturing the full complexity of user interests.

The core problem is multi-stage ad ranking pipelines waste computation by processing candidates that will inevitably be filtered out downstream. The underlying principle is that propagating signals forward and backward across stages—forward to skip expensive final ranking, backward to prevent bad candidates from entering early ranking—eliminates redundant work while preserving quality because you are filtering on the same signals that later stages would use anyway. This principle applies because modern ranking pipelines reuse consistent signals across stages (relevance, expected CTR, quality); if a candidate looks bad at stage one and would look bad at stage three, processing it at stages two and three wastes electricity. Detecting stable signals (those that won't change later) lets you cache results safely. This solves the real problem: computational efficiency—reducing CPU and GPU load without harming user experience by skipping expensive computation on candidates that contribute nothing to the final ranking.

The core problem is that recommendation systems ignore rich semantic content in images and videos, treating multimedia as opaque blobs instead of extracting what is actually shown. The underlying principle is that multimodal models fluent in language and vision can describe multimedia content in words, and those descriptions, when converted to feature tokens, provide semantic signals that older embedding-only approaches miss entirely. This principle applies because users care about what items actually depict (product color, style, materials)—information that is visible in images but invisible to systems that only look at purchase history—and multimodal models trained to understand both modalities learn to extract exactly this kind of content-level information. Converting descriptions to categorical features integrates them with traditional recommendation features cleanly. This solves the practical goal: lifting recommendation quality by incorporating visual and video semantics that have always been present but were going unused.

The core problem is ranking products by similarity when similarity varies by category and context, and naive embedding-based ranking treats all attributes equally. The underlying principle is that extracting structured attributes and arranging them as a graph lets you reason hierarchically about relevance—brand matters for clothing, not for kitchen tools—which grounds reasoning in category-aware structure rather than opaque numerical similarity. This principle applies because product attributes have real categorical meaning that embedding-only models struggle to respect; structured graphs let you weight brand, color, size differently by category, which is how humans actually judge similarity. Using language models to reason over structured graphs costs far fewer tokens than reasoning over raw descriptions because structure eliminates irrelevant words. This solves the practical goal: enabling practical large-scale entity search by reducing per-product inference cost by 57% while improving precision through structured reasoning.

The core problem is that item-based ad targeting fails on broad queries and new items where direct semantic similarity is weak, while keyword targeting succeeds by capturing historical intent but requires manual specification. The underlying principle is that transferring successful query-item pairs from keyword campaigns to item campaigns via learned representations bridges the coverage gap: if a keyword advertiser found that query Q leads to item I, then learning a representation where Q and I are close lets item-based matching surface I for similar queries, solving the sparse case. This principle applies because historical keyword campaigns represent accumulated human wisdom about which queries lead to which items; instead of discarding this knowledge, using it to guide item-based matching compensates for weak direct similarity in broad or new-item cases. Adaptive thresholding lets you admit helpful transfer while rejecting noise. This solves the practical goal: expanding impression coverage on hard-to-match queries and new inventory without sacrificing click quality.

The core problem is recommending travel without reinforcing overcrowded, carbon-intensive destinations, but nudging toward sustainability risks feeling coercive and harming user satisfaction. The underlying principle is that agentic counterfactual explanations—showing users what greener alternatives exist and what tradeoffs they'd face—let users make informed choices rather than being pushed, preserving agency while surfacing the sustainability dimension they may not have considered. This principle applies because humans resist being told what to do but embrace new options when they understand the reasoning; showing a user a sustainable beach resort they genuinely like (not a preachy worse option) is persuasion through evidence, not coercion. Eliciting latent preferences through conversation ensures the system learns what users actually value. This solves the practical goal: scaling sustainable tourism by embedding environmental impact into recommendations without sacrificing the user experience that makes recommendations valuable.

The core problem is that neural ranking models like MonoBERT work well but practitioners cannot see why they rank one item above another, blocking improvement. The underlying principle is that neuron-level gradient analysis reveals which model components contribute most to each decision; by computing how much each neuron's output changes the ranking score when that neuron is slightly perturbed, you expose the contribution map of the entire model. This principle applies because modern ranking models are not mysterious—they are just functions that output scores—and those functions are differentiable, so their sensitivity structure can be measured exactly using calculus; visualization makes this sensitivity concrete. Ablating components then tests whether suspected mechanisms actually matter. This solves the practical goal: making ranking systems auditable and improvable by exposing the internal mechanisms rather than keeping them as black boxes.
